newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS - BPI drops on capital call for BFE.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BPI drops on capital call for BFE.

text.p: Banco Portugues de Investimento shares slumped on Wednesday after announcing a 60 billion escudo capital call to pay for Banco de Fomento & Exterior but further downside was limited, analysts say.
The stock dropped a little over 10 percent to 1,919 escudos with some analysts saying it could stabilise around this level.
Analysts said the 2,615 escudos per share BPI will pay for BFE, valuing the bank at some 210 billion escudos ($1.4 billion), was reasonable.
"It is some 1.4 times book value which is less than has been paid in other recent (Portuguese) bank mergers," said analyst Elizabeth Rothfield of Midas in Lisbon.
Analysts calculated the dilution effect of the capital call on share value at between 10 and 15 percent, meaning that the stock was probably approaching equilibrium point.
BPI will pay the government 136 billion escudos for its 65 percent stake and will then launch a public offer to buy for outstanding stock at the same price.
It has not yet announced full details of the capital call, which will be in two parts, although it has set the ceiling on the amount it seeks to raise.
"I would say that the downside on fundamentals is around five to 10 percent, although I have not had time to check all the figures," said a Lisbon analyst, referring to the BPI share price.
But this analyst, and others, said this did not take account of other factors which could help support the price near-term.

These included the desire of BPI to see its share price perform well ahead of the 30 billion call on existing shareholders which will be made later this year and the fact that, in theory, BPI could be considered a potential takeover target itself.
Analysts said that, while a remote possibility, the figures suggested that it could be financially possible for a predator to launch a bid for BPI on the market and pick up BFE for free.
The capital call will raise BPI's market capitalisation to some 167 billion escudos against the 210 billion at which it values BFE.

"There is room," said an analyst who asked not to be identified. BPI has a core shareholder group that includes German insurer Allianz and Spain's Caja de Ahorros (La Caixa) but even they might not be able to resist a very tempting offer.
However, analysts said an hostile takeover was a dim possibility, not least because of uncertainty over how the Portuguese government would react to any such attempt.
"I believe that BPI could find an equilibrium point between 1,870 and 1,890 escudos. That would be a good buying level," said analyst Pedro Andrada of Lisbon brokers Fincor.
"The price, despite being higher than people had expected, is not really that expensive," added another analyst.
"BPI has succeeded in buying itself the dimension it needed ahead of the changes to come with the introduction of monetary union," added another.
But if BPI, which beat off competition from two local banks, has pulled off a coup in landing BFE, the Portuguese Finance Ministry also has reason to smile.
When the battle for BFE first began, BPI was offering 1,650 escudos per share, some 38 percent below the final price.
